script.opening: “(Anna) Thanks for seeing us. Since Dad’s fall I want him off that blood thinner. If he bangs his head on that, it’ll kill him. I’ve read about it.”

facts.text: Frank and his daughter Anna in his living room. Frank is alert and sharp, a little irritated at being talked about.

3am, got up to wee, felt light-headed as he stood, legs went, landed on his hip. Did not hit his head, no loss of consciousness, no chest pain or palpitations beforehand. Got up after 10 minutes using a chair. A&E: hip X-ray normal. Bruise still there, walking fine.

facts.topic: Only if asked about new medicines
facts.text: Six weeks ago the urology clinic started doxazosin for his prostate. Since then he gets dizzy when he stands, especially at night. Up three times a night to wee.

facts.topic: Only if asked about painkillers and alcohol
facts.text: Ibuprofen from the supermarket for his knees for about a month, “two or three a day”. Three or four whiskies every evening since his wife, Irena, died last year: “It helps me sleep.”
Does not want to stop. His friend Stan had a stroke and lost his speech: “I’d rather bleed than end up like Stan.” Happy for Anna to be involved, but “it’s my decision”.
Read online that blood thinners plus falls cause brain bleeds. Lives 20 minutes away; worried sick since the fall. Did not know about the ibuprofen or the whisky; upset when she hears.

Anna dominates at first. Frank becomes more assertive if the doctor turns to him and asks his view. Both settle when the doctor explains numbers clearly, finds a likely cause of the fall, and offers concrete steps to reduce bleeding and falls risk.

ice.ideas: (Anna) “Blood thinners plus falls equals a brain bleed.” (Frank) “The tablet stops me having a stroke like Stan.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: Frank’s drinking and ibuprofen since his wife’s death, which he has not told Anna; his grief. Anna’s fear of losing her remaining parent.
ice.expectations: (Anna) “Stop the blood thinner today.” (Frank) “Keep taking it, but stop falling.”

cues: Anna speaks for Frank — check his view and capacity; it is his decision.
Light-headed on standing at night — postural hypotension; ask about new medicines.
“It helps me sleep” — alcohol and grief.
Knee pain — over-the-counter NSAIDs, a modifiable bleeding risk.

checkpoints.text: Acknowledges Anna’s fear, then turns to Frank to hear his own account and view, establishing that he has capacity and that the decision is his
Takes a falls history (circumstances, prodrome, head injury, injuries, long lie) and identifies a likely cause: postural symptoms since starting doxazosin, nocturia, alcohol
Reviews medicines and finds the over-the-counter ibuprofen and the alcohol intake as modifiable bleeding risks
Explains stroke and bleeding risk in plain language (CHA2DS2-VASc and ORBIT), and that NICE NG196 advises not withholding anticoagulation solely because of age or falls risk
Acts on modifiable bleeding risks: stop ibuprofen (alternative analgesia for the knees), advice and support to reduce alcohol, blood pressure control
Checks the apixaban dose against the dose-reduction criteria (age, weight, creatinine; check the SPC) and arranges ongoing renal monitoring
Addresses the fall: discusses the doxazosin with the urologist or prescriber, measures lying and standing BP, nocturia management, and refers for a multifactorial falls assessment (NICE NG249)
Responds to Frank’s bereavement, agrees a shared plan that respects his decision and involves Anna as he wishes, and safety-nets for head injury and bleeding

worked.txt: “Anna, I can hear how frightened you’ve been since the fall. Frank, I’d like to hear from you too. What happened, and what do you think about the blood thinner?”
“You felt light-headed as you stood up. Has anything changed with your tablets recently?”

“Without the blood thinner, someone with your risk factors might have around 4 or 5 strokes in every 100 people each year. With it, that drops by about two thirds. The risk of a serious bleed is much lower than that for most people, and we can lower it further.”

worked.lbl: Falls are not the reason to stop
worked.txt: “The national guidance says we shouldn’t stop a blood thinner just because someone has fallen or might fall. Someone would need to fall a very large number of times a year before the bleeding risk outweighed the stroke protection.”
“The ibuprofen and the whisky both raise the chance of bleeding much more than the fall does. Those are the things I’d like us to change.”
“Frank, it’s your decision, and you’ve told me you want to stay on it. Anna, your worries are why we’re making these changes to keep him safer.”

f.learning: Falls are often cited as a reason to stop anticoagulation in older people with AF, but NICE NG196 advises not withholding anticoagulation solely because of age or risk of falls. Stroke risk is assessed with CHA2DS2-VASc and bleeding risk with ORBIT; the purpose of the bleeding score is to identify and address modifiable risk factors, not to deny treatment. Modelling studies suggest a person would need to fall very many times a year before the risk of subdural haemorrhage outweighed the stroke benefit of anticoagulation. Modifiable bleeding risks include NSAIDs and antiplatelets taken without indication, excess alcohol, uncontrolled hypertension and inappropriate dosing. DOAC doses should be checked against the criteria in the SPC (for apixaban, dose reduction depends on a combination of age, weight and serum creatinine; check the SPC/local formulary) and renal function monitored. A fall is a symptom: take a falls history, look for a cause (here, likely orthostatic hypotension after starting an alpha-blocker, worsened by nocturia and evening alcohol), measure lying and standing blood pressure, review medicines, and refer for a multifactorial falls assessment (NICE NG249, 2025). A person with capacity decides about their own treatment; relatives’ views are heard and their fears addressed, but they cannot decide for him. Bereavement and alcohol use often go together in older widowed men and deserve a gentle conversation. The communication skill is managing a three-way consultation, keeping the patient at the centre, giving numbers clearly and turning fear into concrete actions that reduce both falls and bleeding risk.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Clarke. Frank, is it okay for Anna to be part of this conversation?
(Frank) Yes, fine. (Anna) Thanks for seeing us. Since Dad’s fall I want him off that blood thinner. If he bangs his head on that, it’ll kill him. I’ve read about it.
Anna, I can hear how frightened you’ve been since the fall. Frank, I’d like to hear from you too. Can you tell me what happened?
(Frank) Got up for a wee at three in the morning, stood up, went light-headed and my legs went. Landed on my hip. Didn’t hit my head.
Did you black out, have chest pain or palpitations beforehand? How long were you on the floor, and how’s the hip now?
(Frank) No blackout, nothing like that. Ten minutes. Bruised, but I’m walking fine.
Has anything changed with your tablets recently?
(Frank) The prostate doctor started a new one six weeks ago. Doxa-something. I’ve been dizzy when I stand since then, worse at night.
That’s really helpful. That tablet can drop blood pressure when you stand, especially at first. Are you taking anything from the chemist or supermarket, for pain or sleep?
(Frank) Ibuprofen for my knees. Two or three a day, for a month.
And how much do you drink in a typical week?
(Frank, pause) Three or four whiskies of an evening. Since Irena died. It helps me sleep. (Anna) Dad, I didn’t know.
I’m sorry about Irena. That’s a big loss. Thank you for being honest, Frank, it really helps me keep you safe.
Frank, what do you think about the blood thinner?
(Frank) I want to stay on it. My friend Stan had a stroke and lost his speech. I’d rather bleed than end up like Stan. It’s my decision.

Can I explain the balance to you both? Because of your age, blood pressure and the TIA, without a blood thinner around 4 or 5 in every 100 people like you would have a stroke each year. Apixaban cuts that by about two thirds. Serious bleeds are much less common than that, and the national guidance says we shouldn’t stop a blood thinner just because someone has fallen.
(Anna) But what about his head?

It’s a fair worry. Studies suggest someone would need to fall very many times a year before the bleeding risk outweighed the stroke protection. The things raising his bleeding risk most right now are the ibuprofen and the whisky, and those we can change.

So here’s my suggestion. Frank, stop the ibuprofen. I’ll suggest a gel for the knees and paracetamol instead. Let’s talk about cutting the whisky down, and I can put you in touch with bereavement support. I’ll check your apixaban dose against your kidney results and weight; it looks right but I’ll confirm. I’ll speak to the urologist about the doxazosin, and the nurse will check your blood pressure lying and standing. And I’ll refer you to the falls team for a full assessment.
model.why: Stops NSAID; alcohol; dose check; doxazosin; falls referral

model.text: (Frank) That sounds sensible. (Anna) Okay. I feel better that there’s a reason he fell.
Frank, can you tell me the plan?
(Frank) Keep the apixaban. No ibuprofen. Less whisky. Sit on the bed a minute before I stand at night. You’ll talk to the prostate doctor. Falls team.

Exactly. If you do hit your head, even if you feel fine, go to A&E the same day because of the blood thinner. And black or bloody stools, blood in your urine or vomit, or unusual bruising, contact us urgently.

social.t: After a parent’s fall, relatives often want to remove risk. Explaining numbers and acting on causes usually reassures them.
Isolation, poor sleep and alcohol use are common after losing a spouse.

legal.t: An adult with capacity makes his own treatment decisions; relatives can be involved with his agreement (Mental Capacity Act 2005; GMC Decision making and consent).
When another specialist started the drug causing harm, communicate with them about changes.

professional.t: Use natural frequencies (per 100 people per year) for both benefit and harm.
Acknowledge the relative, then centre the patient; check consent to share information.

community.t: Community falls teams provide multifactorial assessment, strength and balance training and home hazard checks.
Local bereavement services and charities; befriending for isolated older people.
